title: Your story needs a buyer question.
caption:
A founder story becomes useful when it helps someone make a decision.

Start with a question your buyer is already asking. Then explain a choice you actually made, the trade-off behind it and the lesson another team can use.

The details matter: what changed, who was affected and what you learned. If a result is still unknown, say so.

What decision do buyers misunderstand about your category?

#FounderLed #B2BSaaS
slides: What is your buyer trying to decide before they can move forward?
Pick a choice your team can describe accurately: what changed and why.
Explain the alternative you considered and what you gave up.
Turn that decision into a principle someone else can test.

title: Make your positioning testable.
caption:
A strong positioning statement should help a buyer work out whether the product is relevant.

Name the customer, the decision or task, and the alternative they would otherwise use. Then explain the meaningful difference with proof you can actually share.

If the sentence could describe five other companies unchanged, it needs another pass.

#Positioning #B2BAI
slides: Who uses the product, and what are they trying to get done?
A spreadsheet, an internal process or another product can all be alternatives.
State one relevant difference. Support it with a demonstration or evidence.
Ask a buyer to repeat it.
Could they explain the product and the relevant alternative in plain words?

title: An AI claim needs a boundary.
caption:
A buyer does not only need to know what an AI product can do. They need to know when it works, how it is checked and where a human remains responsible.

Use a concrete workflow. Identify the input, the output, the review step and the limits. Add measured results only when the method and denominator are available.

The aim is clarity that a buyer can evaluate.

#AIProduct #B2BMarketing
slides: Describe the input, the action and the output a user will see.
Show the review step, escalation path or human decision where relevant.
Be specific about conditions, exclusions and uncertainty.
Use a real example or measured result with its source, period and denominator.

title: Explain the workflow around the model.
caption:
A model name rarely explains what changes in a buyer's day.

Walk through the sequence instead: what starts the workflow, what the system suggests, where a person reviews it and what happens next.

A simple diagram or product screenshot can help when it makes one of those steps clearer. Protect private data and describe only features that exist.

#ProductMarketing #B2BAI
slides: What event or question starts the work?
Describe what the product returns and where a person can inspect it.
What does the team do with the output?
Draw the path in four steps.
Trigger, input, review, action. Label the human decision.

title: One interview. Five useful angles.
caption:
The raw material for good founder content is often already in the team's decisions. The challenge is capturing it with enough context.

In an interview, ask what changed, what the team considered, where the trade-off was difficult and what a buyer should understand.

From there, an editor can propose different angles. The founder checks the wording and evidence before publication.

#FounderContent #ContentStrategy
slides: Ask for the context, the options and the people affected.
The alternative and the reason can make the thinking concrete.
Identify a safe example, a diagram or evidence the team can share.
Turn the answer into a series.
Explain the choice, teach a method, compare options, clarify a limit, or answer an objection.

title: Help buyers compare the options.
caption:
A useful comparison does more than list features. It helps a buyer decide what matters in their own situation.

Offer a checklist: the task, the data required, the review process, integration constraints and the cost of changing course.

Describe alternatives fairly. A comparison earns attention by making a decision easier, not by pretending every team needs the same answer.

#BuyerEnablement #SaaS
slides: What must the team complete, and how will they know it is done?
Consider inputs, security, implementation and the people involved.
Show where each option fits and where it may not.
Give the buyer questions to take into their own evaluation.

title: Two voices. One clear story.
caption:
Founder profiles and company pages can do different jobs while telling the same story.

A founder can explain the reasoning behind a decision. A company page can make the workflow, product changes and permissioned evidence easy to find.

This is an editorial model to test with your own audience. The available sample does not prove that one account type causes better results.

#FounderLed #LinkedInStrategy
slides: Explain why a choice mattered and what the team learned.
Document the product workflow, updates, limitations and approved proof.
The founder's perspective and the company's explanation should reinforce each other.
Use the same account, similar post age and the metrics actually available.

title: Build a calendar around decisions.
caption:
A calendar should make useful ideas easier to publish.

Start with a short list of buyer questions. For each one, identify a founder viewpoint, a piece of evidence and a format that helps explain it.

Then leave room to learn: review comparable posts, listen to real conversations and update the plan when you have better evidence.

#ContentStrategy #B2BMarketing
slides: Use real sales, product and customer conversations where the team has permission.
Match each question to a voice.
Choose the person or company source that can answer it accurately.
Select a diagram, text, document or video for the explanation it enables.
Compare similar posts over the same time window; record questions and limitations.

title: What do LinkedIn reactions tell you?
caption:
A reaction is a visible response such as Like, Celebrate or Insightful. A comment is a separate reply. They are different measures.

In our selected sample of 279 posts, reactions were available for 276 posts. The median was 107.5 reactions. Comments were available for 256 posts; their median was 36.5. Captures took place 20–22 October 2026.

This is a selected reference sample, not a current platform benchmark. We did not observe reach, clicks or conversions, so these figures cannot establish an engagement rate or sales result.

#LinkedInAnalytics #B2BContent
slides: The reaction total combines available reaction types. It does not include comments.
A comment total is not unique people, qualified buyers or sales.
Medians: 276 observed reaction counts; 256 observed comment counts. 279 posts in the selected sample.
We did not observe impressions, reach, clicks or sales. Reactions are not proof of buying intent.

title: Turn a response into a better question.
caption:
A response to a post can tell you what to investigate next. It does not automatically tell you why someone reacted or whether they intend to buy.

Look for the questions people actually ask. Group recurring themes, bring them back to the founder or product team, and use the answer to improve the next piece of content.

When you talk about a customer example, get permission and check the details.

#ContentLearning #FounderLed
slides: Keep reactions, comments and actual buyer conversations as separate measures.
Identify recurring confusion or objections without assigning intent to a reaction.
Bring it to the right expert.
Ask the founder or product team for an accurate answer and source.
Explain the answer, show relevant proof and retain the limits.
